summary: Defines the SIP REFER method, which asks the receiver to contact a resource named in the request, and lets the sender be told how that attempt turned out. This underlies features such as call transfer. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: REFER lets one SIP endpoint ask another endpoint to contact a resource named in the request. The recipient can report the outcome through NOTIFY messages, which supports call transfer and other applications.

subtitle: How a SIP request asks another endpoint to contact a resource and report the result.

tldr.problem: SIP needs a way for one endpoint to ask another to contact a resource and then receive the outcome. Call transfer is one use for this behavior.
tldr.mechanism: A REFER request names the resource in one Refer-To header. If accepted, the recipient attempts the request and sends status updates in NOTIFY messages through an implicit subscription to the refer event.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the REFER method, the Refer-To header, and the refer event package. RFC 3515 is updated by RFC 7647 and RFC 8217.

facts.label: Notification rate
facts.value: SHOULD NOT exceed once per second

today: RFC 3515 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7647 and RFC 8217. Read those updates alongside this document.

sections.title: What the REFER Method Does
sections.content:
REFER is a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) method that asks the recipient to contact a third party or other resource specified in the request. The sender can then be notified about the result. The RFC gives call transfer as an example: Alice can ask Bob's user agent to contact Carol and report whether it succeeded.

REFER implicitly creates a subscription to the refer event. It may be sent outside a dialog created by INVITE, and REFER itself creates a dialog. Unless this RFC states otherwise, a REFER is emitted and answered like a BYE request.
sections.plainLanguage: One SIP endpoint can ask another to contact a named resource. The receiving endpoint can report whether that request succeeded.

sections.title: The Refer-To Header and Approval
sections.content:
A REFER request MUST contain exactly one Refer-To header value. The header holds the URL or URI to contact and has the compact form r. It appears only in REFER requests. The Contact header cannot name the target because Contact is used by SIP's Route and Record-Route mechanism.

A user agent accepting a well-formed REFER SHOULD seek user approval, either interactively or through configured policy. If approval is granted, it MUST contact the URI using the normal mechanism for that URI type. An agent MUST return 400 Bad Request when a REFER has no Refer-To value or more than one.
sections.plainLanguage: Refer-To contains the target, and each REFER must have exactly one target. Before acting, the receiving program should get approval from its user or follow configured policy.

sections.title: Accepting a Request and Reporting Progress
sections.content:
If no earlier response decides the request, the receiving user agent MUST return 202 Accepted before the REFER transaction expires. Acceptance requires the recipient to create a subscription and notify the sender of the reference's status. A subscription created this way triggers an immediate NOTIFY, so the sender must be ready to receive one before the REFER transaction completes.

Each NOTIFY MUST contain Event: refer and a message/sipfrag body beginning with a SIP response status line. That line gives a complete statement of status; the event package does not support state deltas. The final NOTIFY MUST mark the subscription terminated with reason noresource. Notifications SHOULD NOT be sent more than once per second.

If another REFER is sent in the same dialog, the NOTIFY Event header MUST include an id parameter with the REFER's CSeq number so the sender can match each update to its request.
sections.plainLanguage: After accepting REFER, the recipient sends an immediate status message and later sends another when it has an outcome. Each message states the current result, and later REFER requests in the same dialog get an identifier in their updates.

sections.title: Status Lines and a Typical Exchange
sections.content:
The body of each NOTIFY begins with a SIP response status line. The RFC describes a minimal implementation that can report SIP/2.0 100 Trying while pending, SIP/2.0 200 OK on success, SIP/2.0 503 Service Unavailable on failure, or SIP/2.0 603 Declined if approval is later denied.

The example call flow has Agent A send REFER to Agent B. B answers with 202 Accepted, then sends a NOTIFY; A acknowledges it. After B completes the referenced action, B sends a final NOTIFY and A acknowledges that too. A successful status can also be reported for a non-SIP target using a SIP status line.
sections.plainLanguage: The first update can say that the request is underway, and a later update can say it worked or failed. The sender acknowledges each NOTIFY message.

sections.title: Risks of Following and Reporting URIs
sections.content:
A REFER may contain a URI with an arbitrary scheme. A user agent that follows such URIs automatically could be used to attack another host, especially a host behind the same firewall. The RFC recommends showing the full URI when asking for approval; a display name alone is not tied to the URI and is not enough.

NOTIFY bodies can disclose private or confidential information if they copy every response from the referenced action. The RFC recommends returning a carefully selected subset. A status-line-only body reveals the least information.
sections.plainLanguage: A REFER can ask software to open a resource using different kinds of address. The user should see the actual address, and status updates should avoid revealing more information than needed.

sections.title: Why the Result Arrives Later
sections.content:
The method began as TRANSFER and was generalized to REFER. The RFC says this separated transfers from BYE processing, helping with failed-transfer recovery and state management.

Early versions waited for the referenced action to finish before sending a final REFER response. The RFC says that approach did not fit the timeout rules for non-INVITE requests. REFER therefore receives an immediate final response, while NOTIFY carries the later outcome.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipient answers the REFER promptly because waiting for the other action could exceed the request's timeout. Separate NOTIFY messages carry progress and the eventual result.
